title: Episode 128: James K. Polk and the Golden Coast: To the Halls of Montezuma
description:

In eighteen forty-six, President James K. Polk was determined to complete the continental expansion of the United States. Having peacefully secured the Pacific Northwest from Great Britain, Polk set his sights on the vast, sparsely populated territories of northern Mexico: Alta California and New Mexico. When diplomatic overtures to purchase the territories for thirty million dollars were rejected by the Mexican government, border clashes along the Rio Grande ignited the Mexican-American War.

What followed was the most ambitious military campaign the young republic had ever mounted. General Zachary Taylor shattered Santa Anna's army at the Battle of Buena Vista; Captain John C. Frémont launched the Bear Flag Revolt in California; and General Winfield Scott conducted America's first major amphibious landing at Veracruz, fighting his way up the mountain passes along the historic invasion route of Hernán Cortés to capture Mexico City and the citadel of Chapultepec—immortalized as 'the Halls of Montezuma.'

Under the eighteen forty-eight Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Mexico ceded California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and New Mexico to the United States. Just nine days before the treaty was signed, a carpenter named James Marshall spotted glittering flakes of gold in the tailrace of Sutter's Mill in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada. Polk verified the find in his final message to Congress, triggering the legendary California Gold Rush and transforming America into a two-ocean continental empire. Here is George with the epic saga of the Golden Coast.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our exploration of President James K. Polk with the colossal military and geopolitical campaign that completed the continental map of the United States. In eighteen forty-six, Polk led a divided nation into the Mexican-American War. In less than two years, American armies marched to the Pacific Ocean, captured Mexico City, and acquired California. Then, in a twist of providential fortune, the earth opened to reveal the richest gold strike in human history. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: BLOOD ON THE RIO GRANDE
In April eighteen forty-six, the dusty chaparral along the Rio Grande became the flashpoint of North American destiny. Following the annexation of Texas, the United States and Mexico were locked in a bitter border dispute. Mexico claimed that the historic southern boundary of Texas was the Nueces River, while the United States, backing Texas claims, insisted the border was the Rio Grande, one hundred and fifty miles to the south.
President James K. Polk, determined to acquire California and New Mexico, ordered General Zachary Taylor and an army of four thousand regular troops to advance into the disputed territory between the two rivers and erect Fort Texas directly across from the Mexican city of Matamoros. The Mexican commander, General Mariano Arista, viewed the movement as an act of armed invasion. On April twenty-fifth, eighteen forty-six, sixteen hundred Mexican cavalry crossed the Rio Grande, ambushing a patrol of sixty-three American dragoons under Captain Seth Thornton, killing eleven and capturing the rest.
When Taylor's dispatch reached the White House two weeks later, Polk seized the moment. On May eleventh, he sent a fiery war message to Congress, declaring: 'Mexico has passed the boundary of the United States, has invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil.' Despite fierce opposition from Northern Whigs—including a young, lanky freshman congressman from Illinois named Abraham Lincoln, who introduced the 'Spot Resolutions' demanding to know the exact spot of American soil where blood was shed—Congress voted overwhelmingly for war. The clash for the American continent had begun.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BEAR FLAG REVOLT AND THE GOLDEN SHORE
Even before war was officially declared in Washington, Polk had set covert wheels in motion to seize California. Alta California was a vast, enchanting territory of rolling golden hills, Spanish missions, and magnificent natural harbors like San Francisco Bay. But Mexico's hold on the region was gossamer-thin: fewer than eight thousand Mexican Californios and fewer than one thousand American settlers lived scattered across eight hundred miles of coastline.
Operating in California under secret instructions from Polk was Captain John C. Frémont, the charismatic army topographical engineer and explorer known to the nation as 'The Pathfinder.' On June fourteenth, eighteen forty-six, a band of rough American frontiersmen and mountain men, encouraged by Frémont, rode into the town of Sonoma, arrested the Mexican military commandant Mariano Vallejo, and proclaimed the independent California Republic. They raised a homemade cotton flag painted with red berry juice depicting a grizzly bear and a red star—the legendary 'Bear Flag.'
Three weeks later, Commodore John D. Sloat sailed the United States Pacific Squadron into Monterey Bay, raised the Stars and Stripes over the custom house, and claimed California for the United States. Simultaneously, Colonel Stephen Watts Kearny led the 'Army of the West' on an epic one-thousand-mile desert march from Fort Leavenworth, capturing Santa Fe without firing a shot, before pushing across the Gila River desert to link up with naval forces at San Diego. In January eighteen forty-seven, after sharp skirmishes at San Pasqual and Rio San Gabriel, the Treaty of Cahuenga was signed, securing California under American military control.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: OLD ROUGH AND READY AT BUENA VISTA
While California fell, the land war in northern Mexico turned into an epic clash of titans. General Zachary Taylor, nicknamed 'Old Rough and Ready' for his rumpled clothes and unpretentious courage, drove deep into northern Mexico, capturing the fortified stronghold of Monterrey in bloody street-to-street fighting in September eighteen forty-six. Taylor's victories made him a towering national hero, and Whig politicians began openly touting him as their next presidential candidate.
Polk, an intensely partisan Democrat, grew deeply suspicious of Taylor's growing fame. In late eighteen forty-six, Polk stripped Taylor of most of his veteran regular troops, ordering them to join a new expeditionary force under General Winfield Scott. Taylor was left with barely forty-seven hundred raw, untested volunteers to hold the northern front at Saltillo.
Seeing Taylor's vulnerability, the charismatic Mexican dictator, General Antonio López de Santa Anna, assembled a colossal army of twenty thousand soldiers and marched across the barren northern deserts to crush Taylor's small force. On February twenty-second, eighteen forty-seven, the two armies collided in a rugged mountain pass near the hacienda of Buena Vista. Santa Anna sent Taylor a formal summons: surrender at discretion or be cut to pieces. Taylor curtly replied: 'Tell Santa Anna to come and take us.'
For two harrowing days, Taylor's raw volunteers stood against wave after wave of Mexican cavalry and infantry. When the American line buckled on the second afternoon, Taylor rode his famous white horse Old Whitey to the center of the battlefield, sat with one leg casually hooked over his saddle, and shouted to his artillery commander, Captain Braxton Bragg: 'A little more grape, Captain Bragg!' Bragg's flying artillery raked the charging Mexican columns with double canister, breaking Santa Anna's assault. Santa Anna retreated under cover of night, and Zachary Taylor became an unstoppable political legend.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: WINFIELD SCOTT'S EPIC INVASION
Buena Vista secured northern Mexico, but Santa Anna stubbornly refused to negotiate peace. James K. Polk recognized that only the capture of the enemy capital itself could end the war. Command of this master stroke was entrusted to Major General Winfield Scott—'Old Fuss and Feathers'—a towering military genius who stood six feet five inches tall and demanded strict European military discipline.
On March ninth, eighteen forty-seven, Scott executed the first major amphibious landing in United States military history. Operating with the United States Navy, Scott landed twelve thousand troops on the beaches south of Veracruz in specialized surfboats without losing a single man. After a punishing twenty-day siege, the fortress city of Veracruz surrendered, providing Scott with an ocean supply base.
What followed was one of the most audacious military campaigns in world history. With an army of fewer than eleven thousand men, Scott deliberately severed his own supply lines to the coast, marching two hundred and sixty miles through high mountain passes into the heart of an empire of eight million hostile inhabitants. When the Duke of Wellington in London followed Scott's map, the conqueror of Napoleon declared: 'Scott is lost! He cannot win, and he cannot fall back!'
Serving on Scott's staff were brilliant young West Point engineers and artillery officers whose names would soon ring across American history: Captain Robert E. Lee, Lieutenant Ulysses S. Grant, Lieutenant Thomas J. Jackson, Lieutenant George G. Meade, and Captain George B. McClellan. At Cerro Gordo, Robert E. Lee discovered a mountain trail that allowed Scott to outflank Santa Anna's artillery on the heights, shattering the Mexican defenses and clearing the road to the Valley of Mexico.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: TO THE HALLS OF MONTEZUMA
In August eighteen forty-seven, Scott's legions crested the mountain rim and looked down upon the dazzling, sunlit lakes and church spires of Mexico City. Santa Anna had fortified every stone bridge and causeway leading into the ancient Aztec capital with thirty thousand veteran defenders.
In a series of ferocious, bloody battles—Contreras, Churubusco, and Molino del Rey—Scott's soldiers stormed stone monasteries and breached fortified haciendas with cold bayonets. Standing between the Americans and the city gates was the ultimate fortress: Chapultepec Castle, a towering two-hundred-foot volcanic stone citadel that housed the Mexican National Military Academy.
On the morning of September thirteenth, eighteen forty-seven, Scott unleashed a deafening artillery barrage against Chapultepec. At eight o'clock, American assault columns, spearheaded by pickaxes and scaling ladders, scrambled up the sheer, rocky cliffs under withering musket fire. In savage hand-to-hand combat, American soldiers and United States Marines fought room to room through the academy. A group of teenage Mexican cadets, celebrated to this day as Los Niños Héroes, fought to the death, with cadet Juan Escutia wrapping himself in the Mexican flag and leaping from the ramparts rather than surrender.
At nine-thirty in the morning, the Stars and Stripes rose above Chapultepec Castle. American columns fought their way through the San Cosme and Belén gates into the city, with Lieutenant Ulysses S. Grant mounting a light howitzer in the belfry of a church to rake Mexican snipers. At dawn on September fourteenth, General Winfield Scott, mounted on a magnificent horse and surrounded by dragoon sabers, rode into the Grand Plaza of Mexico City, taking possession of the National Palace. It was this historic triumph that forever enshrined the opening words of the Marine Corps Hymn: 'From the Halls of Montezuma to the shores of Tripoli.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TREATY OF GUADALUPE HIDALGO
With Mexico City occupied, Santa Anna resigned the presidency and fled into exile. But negotiating a peace treaty proved an agonizing, bizarre diplomatic drama. Polk's peace commissioner in Mexico, Nicholas Trist, had been ordered by Polk to return to Washington after initial talks stalled. Convinced that departing would leave Mexico in anarchy and prolong the war indefinitely, Trist committed an act of astonishing insubordination: he ignored the President's recall order, remained in Mexico City, and continued secret negotiations with the Mexican interim government.
On February second, eighteen forty-eight, in the historic village of Guadalupe Hidalgo north of Mexico City, Trist and Mexican commissioners signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Under the treaty, Mexico recognized the Rio Grande as the southern border of Texas, and ceded to the United States an enormous expanse of over five hundred and twenty-five thousand square miles—encompassing all of California, Nevada, and Utah, and substantial portions of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, and Wyoming. In return, the United States agreed to pay Mexico fifteen million dollars and assume over three million dollars in private claims of American citizens against Mexico.
When the treaty arrived on Polk's desk, the President was privately furious at Trist's insubordination, later firing him from the State Department. But Polk was a supreme pragmatist: the treaty secured every single territorial objective he had promised the nation. Polk submitted the treaty to the Senate, which ratified it on March tenth, eighteen forty-eight. The United States had officially become a two-ocean continental superpower.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GOLD AT SUTTER'S MILL
Nine days before the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed in Mexico City, an event occurred three thousand miles to the northwest that would reshape the modern world. On the cold morning of January twenty-fourth, eighteen forty-eight, a carpenter from New Jersey named James W. Marshall was inspecting the wooden water wheel and tailrace of a sawmill he was constructing for pioneer John Sutter on the American River at Coloma, California.
Looking down into the shallow, gravelly water, Marshall noticed shimmering yellow flakes. He scooped a handful into his palm, tested the metal with a hammer, and found it malleable and heavy. It was pure virgin gold. Marshall and Sutter swore the workers to secrecy, but the secret could not be kept. Within months, San Francisco was emptied of its inhabitants as sailors abandoned merchant ships, storekeepers locked their doors, and soldiers deserted their posts to dig in the Sierra foothills.
In Washington, rumors of California gold were dismissed as frontier exaggeration until December fifth, eighteen forty-eight, when President James K. Polk delivered his Fourth Annual Message to Congress. Polk formally confirmed the discovery, announcing that federal officers had inspected the mines and determined that 'the accounts of the abundance of gold in that territory are of such an extraordinary character as would scarcely command belief were they not substantiated by authentic reports.'
Polk's official confirmation ignited the California Gold Rush. In eighteen forty-nine, over one hundred thousand 'Forty-Niners' from every corner of the globe flooded into California across mountains, deserts, and oceans, propelling California into statehood in eighteen fifty and cementing America's dominance of the Pacific Rim.
James K. Polk had expanded the United States by over one point two million square miles, won a brilliant foreign war, and presided over the discovery of boundless wealth. He had transformed the United States into the master of the continent, fulfilling the dream of an Empire of Liberty from sea to shining sea.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
James K. Polk's presidency completed the continental expansion of the United States, linking the Atlantic to the Pacific and setting off the California Gold Rush. Next week, we turn to the military hero of that war, America's twelfth President, Zachary Taylor—'Old Rough and Ready'—who rode his horse Old Whitey all the way to the White House and unexpectedly stood firm against Southern threats of secession. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
